spec.description: API performance scorecard for monthly and quarterly reporting. Two pillars — Success Rate and On-Time Rate — graded to RED/YELLOW/GREEN, with per-API detail. See the Method row.

panels.description:
**The worse of the two pillars below.**

Not an average — averaging lets a perfect Success Rate hide a bad On-Time Rate, which is what makes a scorecard easy to ignore. Taking the worse of the two means the grade can only be GREEN when both are genuinely healthy, and it always names its own cause.

This grades **the service as a whole, weighted by requests**. It is not a statement about every individual API — see *APIs needing attention* and the per-API table for that.
panels.title: OVERALL GRADE

panels.description:
**Of every request served this period, what share did the server handle without failing?**

`(requests − 5xx responses) ÷ requests`

4xx is deliberately excluded. Over the measured window 498/401/403 are ~19k responses — expired tokens and permission denials. That is the client behaving as designed against a working server; counting it would penalise the team for its users' auth state. Those codes are shown in the status code panel as context.

GREEN ≥99.9% · YELLOW ≥99.0% · RED below 99.0%

*Shown to the nearest whole percent. The grade and the colour are computed from the exact value — and because the GREEN band (99.9%) is finer than the display, a tile reading 100% can legitimately be YELLOW. Trust the colour over the digits.*
panels.title: 1 · Success Rate  —  GREEN ≥99.9% · YELLOW ≥99.0%

panels.description:
**Of every request served this period, what share finished within ${slo:text}?**

`requests faster than ${slo:text} ÷ requests`

One time bar for every API, set by the **${slo:text}** dropdown at the top — no per-route classification to maintain, and the judgement is visible rather than buried in a config.

Read straight off a histogram bucket, so it is exact rather than interpolated, it stays meaningful on low-traffic APIs, and requests slower than 10s are counted as misses instead of vanishing into the histogram's overflow bucket where percentiles cannot see them.

GREEN ≥99.0% · YELLOW ≥95.0% · RED below 95.0%

*Shown to the nearest whole percent, so a genuine 99.7% reads as 100%. The grade and the colour are computed from the exact value; the per-API table below carries the precise figures.*
panels.title: 2 · On-Time Rate  —  GREEN ≥99.0% · YELLOW ≥95.0%

options.content:
**Two questions, asked of every request in the period. Nothing else feeds the grade.**

| # | Pillar | Exactly what is counted | GREEN | YELLOW | RED |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Success Rate** | requests that did **not** return a 5xx ÷ all requests | ≥99.9% | ≥99.0% | <99.0% |
| 2 | **On-Time Rate** | requests finishing within **${slo:text}** ÷ all requests | ≥99.0% | ≥95.0% | <95.0% |

**OVERALL GRADE = the worse of the two.**

Both come from one metric family — the API's own request histogram. No tracing,
no database or downstream-service signals, nothing that needs interpreting before
it means something.

*The same two rules and the same bands grade each individual API in the table
below, so "why is this API yellow?" has the same answer as "why is the service
yellow?".*

panels.description:
Every request scored in this period, excluding the `/metrics` scrape endpoint — that is Prometheus polling the app, not a product API, and including it would add ~23k always-fast requests that flatter both pillars.

This is the denominator of both scores.
panels.title: Total requests

panels.description:
Average requests per second across the selected period.

Not graded — traffic volume is not something the team controls, and rewarding or punishing it would be meaningless. It is here for context: the same latency under twice the load is an improvement, and that is the main story a month-over-month report should tell.
panels.title: Avg request rate

panels.description:
Total time spent serving requests ÷ number of requests, in whole milliseconds.

The plain mean, deliberately — it is what people actually mean by *how long does this API take*, it needs no explanation, and unlike p95 it cannot hide behind the histogram's 10s top bucket.

Shown for context. The grade uses On-Time Rate instead, because an average conceals distribution: a route averaging 200ms can still miss the bar on one request in twenty.

Truncated at millisecond resolution — 12.7ms reads as 12ms.
panels.title: Avg time per request

panels.description:
APIs with at least **$min_requests** requests this period — enough traffic for a percentage to mean something.

Everything below that gate is listed in the *Not graded* table with the same traffic and timing figures, just no grade.
panels.title: APIs graded

panels.description:
Graded APIs that are **not GREEN** — judged by the same two rules and the same bands as the service headline.

**Read this next to the OVERALL GRADE.** The headline is weighted by requests, so a handful of low-traffic APIs can be in trouble while the service total still reads GREEN. That is not a contradiction — most requests really were fine — but this number and the table below are where the engineering work actually is.
panels.title: APIs needing attention

panels.description:
What share of the selected time range is actually backed by recorded data.

The scorecard reads 5-minute recording-rule output kept for **13 months** in VictoriaMetrics. That history starts on **2026-09-17**; a range reaching further back, or an hour in which the rules were not running, shows up here as missing.

**Below 100% means this report does not cover the full period.**
panels.title: ⚠️ Data coverage

panels.description: Pillar 2 over time. Dips here are what pull the grade down; use them to tell a sustained regression apart from a one-off incident — the two need very different responses.
panels.title: On-Time Rate — GRADED

panels.description:
Pillar 1 over time.

This is very close to flat zero for this service — over a recent 2-day window exactly **one** request in ~762k returned a 500. Treat a completely flat zero with suspicion rather than pride: it usually means failures are being caught and returned as 200 rather than that nothing failed. The Signal check below watches for exactly that.
panels.title: Server errors (5xx) — GRADED

panels.description: Throughput over the period. Context for both pillars; never graded.
panels.title: Request rate

panels.description:
Mean request duration over the period, in whole milliseconds.

Read alongside On-Time Rate: if the mean is flat but On-Time Rate falls, the typical request is fine and the tail has got worse — which points at a specific slow path rather than a general slowdown.
panels.title: Avg time

panels.description:
Every status code the API returned this period.

**Only 5xx counts against the Success Rate.** 4xx is shown here so nothing is hidden, but it is client-side: 498 and 401 are expired or invalid tokens, 403 is a permission denial, 400 is a malformed request. A team cannot fix its users sending stale tokens, and grading it would swamp the real signal — 4xx outnumbers 5xx here by roughly four orders of magnitude.

Worth watching for *changes* though: a sudden 400 spike usually means a client shipped a bad payload.
panels.title: Requests by status code

panels.description:
Fires when the API returned **no 5xx at all** across the whole period.

For a service handling hundreds of thousands of requests, a perfectly flat zero is more often broken error reporting than a flawless run — failures caught and returned as HTTP 200 never reach the status code, and Success Rate then measures nothing while reading 100%.

When this is green, the 5xx signal is at least alive and Pillar 1 can be trusted.

1.text: NO 5xx AT ALL — verify error reporting

panels.title: ⚠️ Signal check — is the error rate believable?

panels.description:
**Every API with at least $min_requests requests this period, graded by exactly the same two rules as the service headline.**

Sorted worst first — the top of this table is the engineering action list.

Total requests, average rate and average time are shown for every API so a low grade can be judged in context: an API serving 300 requests a day at 4s is a very different problem from one serving 400k.

targets.expr:
(
floor(1000 * (sum by (http_route)(sum_over_time(route:http_request_seconds:rate5m{job="$service"}[$__range]))
  / sum by (http_route)(sum_over_time(route:http_requests:rate5m{job="$service"}[$__range]))))
) and on(http_route) (300 * sum by (http_route)(sum_over_time(route:http_requests:rate5m{job="$service"}[$__range])) >= $min_requests)

(
clamp(100 * (1 - (sum by (http_route)(sum_over_time(route:http_5xx:rate5m{job="$service"}[$__range])) or (0 * sum by (http_route)(sum_over_time(route:http_requests:rate5m{job="$service"}[$__range]))))
  / sum by (http_route)(sum_over_time(route:http_requests:rate5m{job="$service"}[$__range]))), 0, 100)
) and on(http_route) (300 * sum by (http_route)(sum_over_time(route:http_requests:rate5m{job="$service"}[$__range])) >= $min_requests)

(
clamp(100 * sum by (http_route)(sum_over_time(route:http_requests_bucket:rate5m{job="$service",le="$slo"}[$__range]))
  / sum by (http_route)(sum_over_time(route:http_requests:rate5m{job="$service"}[$__range])), 0, 100)
) and on(http_route) (300 * sum by (http_route)(sum_over_time(route:http_requests:rate5m{job="$service"}[$__range])) >= $min_requests)

panels.title: Per-API scorecard

panels.description:
**APIs that served fewer than $min_requests requests this period — shown in full, just not scored.**

They are excluded from the grade rather than hidden, because a percentage over a handful of requests is noise: one slow request out of three reads as 67% and would drag the headline down on no real evidence.

The same three figures are given as for graded APIs — total requests, average rate and average time — so a slow endpoint here is still visible and can be acted on by judgement rather than by score. Over a monthly or quarterly window many of these will cross the gate and start being graded automatically.

APIs with no traffic at all in the period are not listed.

targets.expr:
(
floor(1000 * (sum by (http_route)(sum_over_time(route:http_request_seconds:rate5m{job="$service"}[$__range]))
  / sum by (http_route)(sum_over_time(route:http_requests:rate5m{job="$service"}[$__range]))))
) and on(http_route) ((300 * sum by (http_route)(sum_over_time(route:http_requests:rate5m{job="$service"}[$__range])) < $min_requests) and (300 * sum by (http_route)(sum_over_time(route:http_requests:rate5m{job="$service"}[$__range])) > 0))

panels.title: APIs with too little traffic to grade

options.content:
## How this scorecard works

Two questions, asked of every request in the reporting period:

1. **Did it work?**  → Success Rate = requests without a 5xx ÷ all requests
2. **Was it on time?** → On-Time Rate = requests within **${slo:text}** ÷ all requests

**Overall grade = the worse of the two.** Not an average: averaging lets one healthy
pillar hide a broken one, which is how scorecards become wallpaper.

| Pillar | GREEN | YELLOW | RED |
|---|---|---|---|
| Success Rate | ≥99.9% | ≥99.0% | <99.0% |
| On-Time Rate | ≥99.0% | ≥95.0% | <95.0% |

The same two rules and the same bands grade each individual API, so there is one
concept to learn rather than two.

### Where the numbers come from

Everything is derived from a single metric family — the API's own request
histogram (`http_server_request_duration_seconds`). Nothing from tracing,
databases or downstream services feeds the grade: those measure other people's
systems, and mixing them in makes a score no one can act on.

- **Total requests** — every request except the `/metrics` scrape endpoint, which
  is Prometheus polling the app rather than a product API.
- **Avg request rate** — requests per second across the period.
- **Avg time per request** — total time spent ÷ requests served. The plain mean,
  because it needs no explanation. It is context, never graded: an average hides
  distribution, and a route averaging 200ms can still miss the bar once in twenty.
- **On-Time Rate** is read straight off a histogram bucket rather than from a
  percentile. That makes it exact, keeps it meaningful on low-traffic APIs, and
  lets it count requests slower than 10s — those land in the histogram's overflow
  bucket where `histogram_quantile` cannot see them at all.

### Why there is one time bar and not a tier system

An earlier draft sorted routes into tiers (interactive / dashboard / batch) with
its own target each. It was dropped: it required classifying every route by hand,
would not survive contact with a second team, and buried the actual judgement
inside a regex where nobody could see or challenge it.

Instead there is **one number, `${slo:text}`, in a dropdown at the top of the
dashboard**. A team that legitimately runs slower work raises it, and the choice
is visible to everyone reading the report.

The trade-off is honest and worth stating: a genuinely slow-by-design endpoint —
a nightly sync, a materialised-view refresh — will score badly against a single
bar. That is why every API in the table carries its request count, rate and mean
duration: so a low grade can be judged in context instead of blindly actioned.

### Deliberate choices

- **4xx is never graded.** Expired tokens, permission denials and malformed
  requests are the client behaving as designed against a working server. They
  are shown in the status-code panel as context.
- **Minimum sample gate.** An API needs ≥`$min_requests` requests to be graded.
  Below that, a percentage is noise. Those APIs get their own table with the same
  traffic and timing figures.
- **Request-weighted headline.** The overall grade reflects what most requests
  actually experienced. A few low-traffic APIs can be unhealthy while the headline
  is GREEN — that is why *APIs needing attention* sits beside it.

### Where the history lives

Prometheus evaluates five recording rules every 5 minutes (route × bucket, with
`/metrics` already excluded) and ships only their output to **VictoriaMetrics**,
which keeps it for **13 months**. Every panel here reads those recorded series, so
a quarter is as cheap to query as a day, and the grade is identical whichever
store answers. Recorded history begins **2026-09-17**. The **Data coverage** panel
states what share of the selected range is genuinely backed by data — check it
before quoting a monthly or quarterly figure.
